_doc: Day-by-day narrative + companions for the Japan trip. Day 1 = 2026-04-18 (land day). Day 10 = 2026-04-27 (return). Team members are pseudonymized for privacy.

trip.title: Japan — April 2026
trip.tagline: A long way to get there, and worth every step.
trip.intro: Bryan was nervous. Everyone he'd talked to about Japan called it their biggest culture shock with any new country. He couldn't agree more. The Caribbean is a cruise. Europe is confusing but navigable. Japan was an alien world — and that was the point. The trip was a work trip with personal exploration on both ends. First time in Japan. The hardest culture shock of his life. And the most rewarding.
trip.team: Six people, six passports. Five internal experts from five different countries — Bryan's manager, the director of product, the Japan customer success manager, the chief researcher, and Bryan — plus the manager's wife, a sixth nationality. Bryan originally took the Japan account for no commission, just to learn it and write it on a resume. The business exploded; he barely slid into the trip and is so glad he did. Young, niche, hungry. Top of the game at very specific things.
trip.stakes: Small company, few resources. Everyone knew if the trip didn't produce, there wouldn't be another one like it. A handful of existing customers, a handful of partners, a handful of key prospects — enough to work with. Bryan was the energy guy. He took that seriously.
trip.discipline: Almost clean of everything for the trip. Caffeine and nicotine. No prescriptions, not even allergy meds. Zyns and multivitamins were the only risks taken in a country with very strict laws. Needed to be sharp intellectually, emotionally, physically, spiritually — all at once, which is almost impossible. Something usually gives. He gave it a real go.
trip.routine: 5 AM wake-up. Meditation, 10 minutes — letting thoughts come and go. Then plan the day: how am I feeling, what do I need to do, what do I want to do. Walk to the only thing open — 7-Eleven, Lawson, or Family Mart. Rice triangles (rice and beans, or rice and tuna, $1-2). Coffee chat with whoever was behind the counter if no one was in line. Wander the city at dawn when it was almost his. Gym opens at 6 (he tried to start at 5:30 the first day and got politely redirected by the front desk). Mostly upper body and stretching — stretch the Shinto out, no dumb middle-aged injury. Public bath after, once or twice a day. L-shaped hot tub, fully nude, shower first, no chlorine, water hot as hell. Felt like heaven after a day of walking. Hotel breakfast at 7, usually first in. After Day 2, switched from Japanese to greek-yogurt + fruit + eggs + bread — every other meal would be fish and meat, fiber needed to come from somewhere.
trip.wandering: Get lost on purpose. Wander best with an interesting target — weave and turn to get there. The most ADHD exploring: see something in the distance, walk that way, two-hour detour, eventually back on course.
trip.standing_out: Couldn't blend in. Towered over everyone. Few Americans on the streets, none as tall. Stares were rare and mostly came from little kids — wanted to make faces, never did. Quiet, respectful, leave a small trace. Asked locals to correct his pronunciation when they were up for it. Got offered silverware once and was briefly offended before realizing only tourist spots even kept silverware out.
trip.this_is_the_way: Everything in Japan was efficient by design. Lines marked. No confusion. Got pointed back to a line marker by an older Japanese woman once — was six inches off. Respectfully moved six inches left. Saw maybe four people jaywalk all trip. Felt Apple-like — minimalist by intent, not by lack. Rules exist for a reason; the reason is things go the way they're supposed to.
trip.food: Surprisingly little seasoning. Bryan thought maybe it was the quality — high-quality meat doesn't need to be hidden. Probably also the minimalist design ethos: cook it perfectly, let it stand. Salt and a few spices, that was it. Raw egg as a dipping sauce — hot meat dunked in just-warm raw egg — was a revelation. Said no to chicken hearts (other organs and cartilage already done; stomach asked for a break). Matcha everywhere. Tea everywhere. Coffee kept him moving.
trip.team_rhythm: Met around 9 most mornings, after his routine. Doug sometimes came straight from bed, working on his laptop. High-profile meetings meant nerves, translations, edits and re-edits. New solution pitch being built mid-trip. Out till 9 or 10 most nights. A couple of late ones. Called Kel most nights when he got back. Clair was the team's walking yelp — Google-Map-pinned restaurants planned weeks ahead, perfect for a Director of Product doubling as restaurant chauffeur. They waited in a lot of organized lines. He hated standing and waiting. The food was always worth it.

days.title: Land + Ginza first night
days.opening_quote: A long way to get there, and worth every step.
days.summary: Lands at HND 15:55, fourteen and a half hours of flying still in the bones. Passport panic at immigration — turned out to be buried deep in a pocket, not lost. A two-machine immigration ritual no foreigner seemed to crack on the first try. The train station gets worse: dozes off mid-rush-hour, looks up at Google Maps and is twenty minutes south of where he should be. Reverses course, gives up on trains, books a hotel. Planes, trains, and literally automobiles. A thirty-minute airport trip turned into three hours — the foretelling for the whole trip: a long way to get there, worth every step. Shower, hits the streets. Tokyo lands like an alien world: NYC vibes with shrines tucked between high-rises, tiny restaurants lining the alleys. First meal: sits down and cautiously watches other people eat before starting. Discovers Kabuki-za next door at 22:16.

days.title: Tsukiji to Senso-ji to Park
days.summary: A 15-hour cross-Tokyo Sunday. Met up with crew that morning — they had their own plans, gave city tips, sent him wandering. Pre-dawn Tsukiji. Then Nakamise-dori climbing toward Senso-ji, vendor-lined and jammed. First shrine ritual: 100 yen (about 68 cents), one bow, two claps, prayer, one more bow. Eavesdropped on every tour guide that passed. Drew his first omikuji from the cylinder of numbered wooden rods — #31. Pulled the slip. THE LEAST FORTUNATE. Lowest of the low. After the initial flash of 'burn it,' decided to keep it — the most ridiculous, on-the-nose first-fortune in Japan, treasured. Then Meiji Jingu's camphor tree and ema wall, where he drew a second omikuji 'from the empress' — better luck, but the first stays his favorite. ADHD wandering filled the gaps: see something in the distance, walk that way, two-hour detour, then back on course. Capped with a drugstore haul.
